kp.k: Reported legal-sector generative AI use nearly doubled
kp.d: CILEX reports Thomson Reuters research showing that generative AI use by legal services organisations increased from 14% in 2024 to 26% in 2025. The release does not provide the research methodology or sample size.
qs: Use of generative AI by legal services organisations has doubled over the last year, from 14% in 2024 to 26% in 2025, according to research by Thomson Reuters.

kp.k: Professionals expect AI centrality despite limited training
kp.d: According to the Thomson Reuters research as reported by CILEX, 78% of legal professionals expect AI to become central to their work within five years, while fewer than half of legal organisations provide staff with AI training. The release presents this mismatch as a significant training gap.
qs: It found that 78% of legal professionals expect AI to become central to their work within five years, yet a considerable training gap exists, with less than half of legal organisations providing AI training to staff.

kp.k: CILEX launches personalised legal AI training academy
kp.d: CILEX has partnered with the AI-powered learning platform 5Mins.ai to provide personalised AI training for legal professionals. The academy is directed at law firms and legal teams and is intended to build staff AI literacy through modules that change alongside the technology.
qs: CILEX (The Chartered Institute of Legal Executives) has partnered with AI-powered online learning platform 5Mins.ai to launch the CILEX AI Academy, delivering personalised AI training to legal professionals.

The CILEX AI Academy is designed to enable law firms and legal teams to equip staff with the skills they need for AI literacy, incorporating modules that evolve to keep pace with the rapidly changing AI landscape and that champion ethical and responsible use of AI.

kp.k: Training combines technical skills with professional safeguards
kp.d: The academy covers generative AI tools and prompt engineering alongside ethics, data security and professional responsibility. CILEX frames AI competence as requiring both practical proficiency and management of risks to legal organisations and their clients.
qs: The online training platform delivers bite-sized sessions on generative AI tools, prompt engineering, AI ethics, data security and professional responsibility.
It allows employees to master emerging AI technologies whilst managing the associated risks to ensure both the organisation and its clients are protected.

kp.k: Smaller legal organisations risk falling behind
kp.d: CILEX commercial director Toby Moseley argues that organisations outside the UK's largest firms may struggle to track AI developments and upskill staff. This is his assessment rather than a finding supported by additional evidence in the release.
qs: No one doubts the significant impact AI is having on the legal sector but outside the UK's largest firms, many risk getting left behind as they struggle to keep on top of new developments and the urgent need to upskill staff.

kp.k: Rapid change challenges traditional training models
kp.d: Moseley contends that conventional training may not update quickly enough for AI's pace of change. He presents continuously evolving content as the academy's response to that limitation.
qs: Traditional training options aren't always able to keep up with the pace of change, so the new academy is designed to evolve to ensure that employees are trained on the most up-to-the-minute information.

kp.k: AI literacy includes hallucination, confidentiality and ethics
kp.d: Moseley identifies hallucinations, confidentiality and ethics as prominent risks requiring workforce preparation. The stated objective is organisation-wide understanding and confident, safe and ethical navigation of AI, rather than merely teaching tool operation.
qs: With concerns about AI hallucinations, confidentiality and ethics front of mind, the AI Academy focuses on giving employees the confidence to navigate AI ethically and safely, cultivating a culture where AI is understood across the organisation.

kp.k: Vendor predicts rapid, low-investment workforce upskilling
kp.d: 5Mins.ai CEO Saurav Chopra claims that the academy can create AI-literate legal teams within weeks, while avoiding lengthy development and substantial technology investment. This is a promotional vendor prediction; the release supplies no outcome evidence validating the proposed timeframe or investment claim.
qs: CILEX AI Academy means employers will be able to build genuinely AI-literate teams in weeks, not years, providing employees with cutting-edge skills and future-proofing their organisations without the need for lengthy build times or significant tech investment.

kp.k: AI mastery must preserve legal professional obligations
kp.d: Chopra frames legal AI adoption as conditional on protecting client confidentiality and maintaining professional standards. This positions professional responsibility as a constraint on, and necessary component of, legal-sector AI competence.
qs: Legal professionals need to master AI tools without compromising client confidentiality or professional standards.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: CILEX reports growing generative-AI adoption and an expectation that AI will become central to legal work, alongside a training shortfall.
pts.d: The release attributes to Thomson Reuters research an increase in organisational generative-AI use from 14% in 2024 to 26% in 2025, describing this as having doubled. It also reports that 78% of legal professionals expect AI to become central to their work within five years, while fewer than half of legal organisations provide AI training. The centrality figure measures respondents' expectations rather than an observed change in work.

pts.k: Toby Moseley claims that rapid AI change risks leaving firms outside the UK's largest firms behind and requires continuously updated staff training.
pts.d: CILEX's commercial director characterises AI as already significantly affecting the legal sector. He identifies keeping up with developments and urgently upskilling staff as challenges, particularly outside the largest UK firms, and says traditional training cannot always keep pace. He presents the academy's evolving content as a response.

pts.k: CILEX presents AI literacy and risk-management training as enabling legal staff to use emerging AI tools while protecting organisations and clients.
pts.d: The release says the academy teaches generative-AI tools, prompt engineering, ethics, data security and professional responsibility. Moseley specifically identifies hallucinations, confidentiality and ethics as concerns and describes the intended outcome as confident, safe and ethical use with organisation-wide understanding. These are claimed training benefits and design objectives, not reported outcomes from an evaluation.

pts.k: Saurav Chopra predicts that the academy will enable employers to build AI-literate legal teams in weeks without lengthy development or significant technology investment.
pts.d: The 5Mins.ai founder and CEO says legal professionals must master AI without compromising confidentiality or professional standards. He attributes the platform's proposed training capability to social-media-style engagement mechanics and content designed by legal AI experts, and claims it will equip employees with current skills and future-proof organisations.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Adoption and expectations claims are attributed to Thomson Reuters research; claims about competitive risk and academy benefits rest on the release's descriptions and named executives' statements.
pts.d: The release supplies percentages for adoption, expected centrality and training provision, but does not identify the research title, sample, geography or methodology. Moseley's claims about firms falling behind and training keeping pace are presented as executive assessments without supporting cases or additional data. Chopra offers platform features and expert-designed content as the explanation for rapid learning, but the document provides no learning-outcome measurements, completion data, cost comparisons or evidence of reduced AI-related incidents.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The release distinguishes recent adoption growth, a five-year expectation horizon, an immediate upskilling need and a claimed weeks-long training period.
pts.d: Published on 16 September 2025, the release compares adoption in 2024 and 2025. The reported expectation that AI will become central is within five years, approximately 2030 in the release's context, although the underlying survey date is not given. Moseley describes current competitive risks and an urgent training need. Chopra's 'weeks, not years' prediction concerns employers using the academy; no course intensity, baseline skill level or definition of achieved AI literacy is specified. Maintaining current skills is tied to evolving training content, and mastery is framed as needing to preserve confidentiality and professional standards.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern legal professionals, law firms and legal teams as learners and employers, with particular concern for firms outside the UK's largest and indirect protection benefits for clients.
pts.d: Legal professionals are expected to encounter AI as a central part of work and need AI literacy and safe-use skills. Law firms and legal teams are the intended purchasers or organisers of staff training, with employers promised rapid capability-building and limited technology investment. Moseley singles out those outside the UK's largest firms as at risk of falling behind. Organisations and clients are described as beneficiaries of better risk management, especially around confidentiality, ethics and professional responsibility. The release does not predict lawyer displacement, staffing changes, pricing changes or access-to-justice effects.
